To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the LMDP problem is fundamentally hard; (b) under certain assumptions, the problem is solvable with polynomial number of episodes; and (c) under stronger assumptions, the problem becomes solvable with no initialization.

1) the regret minimization for LMDPs is in general impossible, 2) if the system dynamics are sufficiently separated from each other, the agent can learn good policies with polynomial regret, 3) if the system satisfies the standard PSR sufficiency assumption and a reachability condition, the regret minimization is solvable with polynomial regret without any initialization.

1) we show that a general class of LMDPs is hard to learn, 2) we show that under sufficient separation, the problem becomes easy to learn, and 3) we show that with additional assumptions (PSR and reachability), we can learn the optimal policy in polynomial time without initialization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much information about the MDP is needed to achieve sublinear regret in LMDPs.

the following questions: 1) How many episodes are required to learn a good policy? 2) How many episodes does it take if the MDP system is separable? 3) How many episodes can we save if we are provided with a good initialization?
the following question: \emph{Can we learn good policies in LMDPs efficiently and with low regret?} We provide positive and negative answers to this question under different assumptions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of any assumptions, LMDPs are hard to learn, but if we assume a separation condition between MDPs, then we can learn efficiently.

, for a general instance of an LMDP with a large $M$, we cannot hope to learn good policies in polynomial number of episodes without any assumptions, but with sufficient assumptions, we can learn good policies with polynomial number of episodes, and the key is a notion of system separation.

(1) if there is no separation in the system dynamics, then the problem is hard and requires at least polynomial number of episodes, (2) if there is some separation, then the problem can be solved efficiently, but requires a good initialization, and (3) if the system dynamics are sufficiently separated, then the initialization can be removed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide an efficient and provably good algorithm for LMDPs, under sufficient separation assumptions, which is also the first algorithm that is shown to be provably good under the PSR assumptions.
the regret minimization for RL in LMDPs can be achieved efficiently if we have a good initialization or the system dynamics are sufficiently separated.
, we provide a regret guarantee and a lower bound for the RL problem in latent MDPs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regret minimization for LMDPs is a hard learning problem in general, but it is possible to design efficient algorithms with polynomial sample complexity when the MDP system is separated.
in the absence of any separation, even learning to be as good as a random policy requires exponential number of episodes in the number of MDPs in the system.
the problem of regret minimization in LMDPs is significantly harder than in MDPs and requires a different algorithmic approach, which is not possible with the standard MDP-based algorithms.
